title: Rate limits and backpressure
summary: Keep a busy service from taking too much work. Compare a request limit with a signal to slow down, then trace a small JavaScript model.
introduction: A library desk can serve only so many people at once. If everyone pushes forward, nobody gets a good turn. A system also needs a clear rule for how much work it can accept.
learningObjectives: Explain a rate limit with a small time window
Describe backpressure and a bounded waiting queue
Trace allowed and delayed requests in a model

blocks.text: Two ways to protect a busy service

A **rate limit** allows only a certain number of requests in a time period. Our example allows one learner to start three searches in any rolling 60 seconds. A rolling window moves forward with the clock.

**Backpressure** means telling the part sending work to slow down because the next part is full. Think of a librarian saying, "Please wait until this tray has room." A rate limit sets a rule; backpressure reacts to how much work is waiting.
The rule should say what it counts: one person, one API key, or the whole service. A limit per person is useful for fairness, but the service still needs a total capacity limit.

items: At 0 seconds, accept the first search. One spot is used.
At 10 and 20 seconds, accept two more. All three spots are used.
At 30 seconds, ask the learner to wait. Do not add this rejected request to the accepted list.
At 60 seconds, the request from 0 seconds leaves our window. Accept the new request.

blocks.title: Small JavaScript model
blocks.caption: This model uses made-up values in your browser. It does not contact a service.

blocks.text: In this model, a request exactly 60 seconds old no longer counts. The clock moves only when the next made-up request is checked. There are no real timers or network requests.
Plan what happens when the limit is reached

rows: A learner makes too many requests
Return HTTP 429, which means too many requests. When possible, include a Retry-After wait time.
Reject extra work clearly, often with HTTP 503, rather than pretending to accept it.
A worker queue reaches its limit
Pause the producer or reject new jobs until there is room. Keep a maximum wait time too.

blocks.text: A queue with no size limit can fill memory and make people wait for old, useless work. A bounded queue has a maximum size. Choose which work may wait and which work needs a quick answer.
Know the limits of this model

The array covers one learner on one computer. A real service with several servers needs shared counters, or another coordinated rule. Checking and updating a counter must happen safely together, so two servers do not use the same last spot.
An IP address can be shared by a whole school. Treating every shared address as one person may block innocent users. Choose fair rules and measure how often valid requests are rejected.

items: Change the final request time from 60 to 59. Predict the last line before running.
The last line becomes 59s wait. All three earlier accepted requests are still less than 60 seconds old.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not retry rejected work right away in a tight loop. Respect the wait time, limit retries, and stop work that is no longer needed.
